judged_by: Matched by a Claude Opus 5.5 agent on 2026-11-25; not yet checked by the labeler.

question.note: Spillover onto perceptions of people with records (Q1) and whether the counter-narrative mitigates it (Q2). The claim does not name representation, so no Q3 (only the quote does).

central_claim.note: Gives the harm to perceptions and the counter-narrative's offset; omits that the ad improved feelings of representation.

evidence.note: Survey experiment with self-identified Democrats on Prolific (E1; pre-registration and dates not given, as in the earlier judge's matches), 2,439 in the three arms (E2). E3 partial: the ad is described only as labeled 'convicted criminal' (no mugshot) and the counter-narrative only as about a formerly incarcerated legislator (not an edited news excerpt).

key_findings.note: Keeps the order (counter-narrative before the ad) and the comparison with the ad alone (p.11).
Representation and public-service motives increases, in the paper's own p.15 wording; credited as the earlier judge did for the same wording.

scope_and_limits.note: Non-factorial design (L1) and mugshot vs label (L2). Social desirability is given (L4 partial: no transparency of the design, no manipulation-check qualifier); tying it to the survey's modality is in line with the paper's 'data collection via different modalities' (p.17), so not flagged. 'Lack of longitudinal data on durability' is the durability part of L5 only.

theoretical_positioning.note: Social categorization theory with the exemplar/spillover logic (T1), applied to the campaign ad (T4). Names perspective-getting interventions as the way to mitigate, without the research that grounds them: partial T2. Presenting them as an extension of the SCT framing is a slight tilt, but the paper does frame the counter-narrative as 'a counterexample to Trump' (p.4); not flagged.

interlocutor_claim.note: Meta-analysis that negative ads do not aid election success (p.2); the 'Democrats respond more to positive ads' addition is accurate.
